## Definition

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{	imes}$, $d,n\ge0$, and $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Let $\Lambda(d,n)$ be the set of weak compositions $\mu=(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_d)$ of $n$ (so $\mu_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ and $\sum_i\mu_i=n$; zero parts are allowed and give empty rows). For $\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)$ let $m_\mu=\sum_{w\in S_\mu}T_w$ ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]) and let $M^{\mu}:=m_\mu H$ be the right ideal it generates, the **(Hecke) permutation module**; $M^{\mu}$ is free over $R$ with basis $\{m_\mu T_{d(t)}:t	ext{ row-standard }\mu	ext{-tableau}\}$ and is the Hecke analogue of the module induced from the trivial representation of the Young subgroup ([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]]).

For a weak composition $\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)$, define $T_0(\lambda,\mu)$ to be the fillings of $[\lambda]$ by $1,\ldots,d$ with exactly $\mu_i$ entries equal to $i$, weakly increasing rows and strictly increasing columns. Put $T_0(\lambda)= igcup_{\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)}T_0(\lambda,\mu)$ and $K_{\lambda\mu}:=|T_0(\lambda,\mu)|$. This explicitly extends the partition-content definition of [[def-semistandard-tableau-and-kostka-number]] to weak compositions, including internal zero counts; a zero count means that its label is absent. The set is finite, since at most $d^n$ fillings occur for $n>0$, and at $n=0$ its unique member is the empty filling.

Here is the freeness statement in detail: the cosets $S_\mu d$ with $d\in D_\mu$ partition $S_n$, and $\ell(ud)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)$ for $u\in S_\mu$, $d\in D_\mu$ ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]), so the standard basis theorem ([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]) gives $T_uT_{d(t)}=T_{ud(t)}$ and $m_\mu T_{d(t)}=\sum_{u\in S_\mu}T_{u\,d(t)}$; these are the standard basis elements indexed by the single coset $S_\mu d(t)$, and the cosets are disjoint, whence $M^\mu= igoplus_tR\,m_\mu T_{d(t)}$ is free with the displayed basis as $t$ runs over the row-standard $\mu$-tableaux.

Put $M:= igoplus_{\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)}M^{\mu}$ ([[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]]) and define the **q-Schur algebra** $$S(d,n):=\mathrm{End}_H(M),$$ the $R$-algebra of right $H$-module endomorphisms of $M$ ([[def-left-and-right-modules]]).

**Cellular structure.** For all $\mu,
u\in\Lambda(d,n)$, $\mathrm{Hom}_H(M^{
u},M^{\mu})$ is free with the semistandard-pair basis constructed below; for every partition $\lambda$ of $n$ with at most $d$ parts and all semistandard $\lambda$-tableaux $S,T$ there is an element $\varphi_{ST}\in S(d,n)$ ([[def-semistandard-tableau-and-kostka-number]]), and the family $$\{\varphi_{ST}:\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n),\ S,T\in T_0(\lambda)\},$$ where $\Lambda^{+}(d,n)$ is the set of partitions of $n$ with at most $d$ parts ordered by dominance $\unrhd$ ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]), is an $R$-basis of $S(d,n)$; the map $\varphi_{ST}\mapsto\varphi_{TS}$ is an algebra anti-automorphism and the triangular axiom holds modulo the span of the $\varphi_{UV}$ with $\muhd\lambda$. Hence $(\varphi,\Lambda^{+}(d,n))$ is a dominance-cellular basis of $S(d,n)$ ([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]) and its cell modules are the **Weyl modules** $W^{\lambda}$, free over $R$ with basis $\{\varphi_T:T\in T_0(\lambda)\}$. Over a field $F$, $W^{\lambda}$ has nonzero simple head $L^{\lambda}$, the $L^{\lambda}$ for $\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n)$ form a complete set of pairwise non-isomorphic absolutely irreducible $S(d,n)$-modules, and the decomposition matrix satisfies $d_{\lambda\lambda}=1$ and $d_{\lambda\mu}

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The commutative ring $R$, its unit $q$, the finite Hecke algebra $H$, its row ideals $M^\mu=m_\mu H$, and $S=\operatorname{End}_H( igoplus_\mu M^\mu)$ in the Definition. Multiplication in $S$ is ordinary composition: $(fg)(x)=f(g(x))$.

[F1] The standard Hecke basis and the length-additive distinguished coset representatives give $m_\mu T_d=\sum_{u\in S_\mu}T_{ud}$ and $m_\mu T_i=q m_\mu$ for each adjacent generator of $S_\mu$ ([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]], [[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]). The involution satisfies $T_w^*=T_{w^{-1}}$ and $m_\mu^*=m_\mu$.

[F2] The proved integral permutation-module basis is $m_{(S,t)}=\sum_{s:\,\mu(s)=S}m_{st}$, with $S$ semistandard of type $\mu$ and $t$ standard of the same shape ([[lem-type-a-hecke-permutation-modules-have-semistandard-murphy-bases-and-specht-filtrations]]). Thus, in Murphy coordinates, membership in $M^\mu$ means that the first tableau has semistandard type $\mu$, its coefficient is constant on each first-index fibre, and every other coefficient is zero. This is the exact basis assertion, over every $R$ and unit $q$, rather than an inference from coset freeness.

[F3] The Murphy elements form an integral cellular basis of $H$. In particular $m_{st}h\equiv\sum_v r_{tv}(h)m_{sv}$ modulo the span $I^{hd\lambda}$ of strictly dominant shapes, with $r_{tv}(h)$ independent of $s$ ([[thm-murphy-tableau-elements-form-a-cellular-basis]]).

[F4] For a finite-dimensional cellular algebra over a field, its nonzero cell-form quotients are a complete set of distinct absolutely simple modules and are simple heads; their decomposition numbers satisfy diagonal $1$ and dominance support ([[thm-nonzero-cell-heads-classify-the-simple-modules-of-a-cellular-algebra]], clause 1 of [[lem-finite-cellular-nonzero-form-heads-purity-and-shared-factor-linkage]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The integral Hom test. The cyclic right module $M^
u$ has presentation $H/\sum_i(T_i-q)H$, where $i$ ranges over the generators of $S_
u$. Indeed, a length-additive decomposition $w=ud$ reduces $T_w$ in this quotient to $q^{\ell(u)}T_d$, and the map $T_d\mapsto m_
u T_d$ maps the resulting spanning family bijectively to the independent disjoint-coset basis. Therefore evaluation at $m_
u$ identifies $\operatorname{Hom}_H(M^
u,M^\mu)$ with the elements $y\in M^\mu$ satisfying $yT_i=qy$ for those generators. Pairing $T_w,T_{ws_i}$ with $\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1$ in the standard basis shows that this equation forces their two coefficients to be equal: the coefficient equations are $qb=qa$ and $a+(q-1)b=qb$, so $a=b$ since $q$ is a unit. Requiring all these equalities makes the coefficients constant on each right $S_
u$-coset. Its unweighted coset sum is $T_c m_
u$ for the minimal right-coset representative $c$, by length additivity. Hence this simultaneous right eigenspace is $Hm_
u=(M^
u)^*$, over every coefficient ring. Evaluation consequently gives an isomorphism $\operatorname{Hom}_H(M^
u,M^\mu)\cong M^\mu\cap Hm_
u$. For $y=a m_
u$ its inverse is $m_
u h\mapsto yh$, which is well defined because $m_
u h=0$ implies $yh=a m_
u h=0$. [given, F1, algebra, construct]

2.1 The semistandard intersection. Expand $y\in H$ uniquely in the Murphy basis. By [F2], membership in $M^\mu$ requires zero coefficients outside semistandard first-index fibres and constant coefficients inside each fibre. Apply $*$ to [F2] to see that membership in $Hm_
u$ imposes the identical condition on the second-index fibres of type $
u$. The two requirements together say precisely that the coefficients are constant on each rectangle $\{(s,t):\mu(s)=S,
u(t)=T\}$, and zero outside these rectangles. Thus their unweighted sums $m_{ST}$ form a basis of the intersection. The rectangles are disjoint and have a coefficient $1$ at every member, so independence and coefficient extraction hold over arbitrary $R$, including singular parameters; no quantum factorial is cancelled. Every nonempty rectangle has shape with at most $d$ rows, since a strictly increasing column can use only $d$ labels. Combining this with step 1.1 gives exactly the maps $\varphi_{ST}$ and the asserted basis of each Hom block, hence of $S$. The construction also commutes with arbitrary base change, because the same free basis and formulas describe each specialized Hom block. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra, construct]

u\cap Hm_\mu$, and extend linearly to $S$. Step 2.1 gives $\varphi_{ST}^*=\varphi_{TS}$, so this is an involution. To check reversal, let $f:M^
u	o M^\mu$ have $f(m_
u)=a m_
u$ and $g:M^\kappa	o M^
u$ have $g(m_\kappa)=b m_\kappa=m_
u h$. Then $(fg)(m_\kappa)=a b m_\kappa$, so $(fg)^*(m_\mu)=m_\kappa b^*a^*$. On the other hand $f^*(m_\mu)=m_
u a^*$ and $g^*(m_
u)=m_\kappa b^*$, whence $(g^*f^*)(m_\mu)=m_\kappa b^*a^*$. Noncomposable blocks give zero on both sides. Since each block map is determined by its generating element, $(fg)^*=g^*f^*$ as claimed. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The cellular multiplication law. Fix $T$ of shape $\lambda$ and type $
u$, and first take $f:M^\kappa	o M^
u$. Write $f(m_\kappa)=m_
u h$. Then $(\varphi_{ST}f)(m_\kappa)=m_{ST}h$. By [F3], its shape-$\lambda$ Murphy coefficient at $(s,v)$ is $\sum_{t:
u(t)=T}r_{tv}(h)$ if $\mu(s)=S$, and zero otherwise; all remaining shapes strictly dominate $\lambda$. This coefficient is independent of $s$. The full element lies in $M^\mu\cap Hm_\kappa$ by step 1.1, so step 2.1 forces these coefficients to be constant on semistandard second-index fibres $\kappa(v)=V$ and zero on the other fibres. For a fixed $T,h$, these constants are independent of $S$: choose any member $s$ of its nonempty first fibre and read the displayed sum, which contains no $s$. Calling the constants $r_V$, evaluation and the intersection basis give $\varphi_{ST}f\equiv\sum_{V\in T_0(\lambda,\kappa)}r_V\varphi_{SV}$ modulo the span of strictly dominant Schur shapes, for every $S$. Sum over Hom blocks for arbitrary $f\in S$. Step 3.1 gives the corresponding left law, so each upward span is a two-sided ideal and the cellular axioms hold. This proves cellularity by actual composition and Murphy coefficient comparison. [F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Partition projections and nonzero forms. For the canonical semistandard tableau $T^\lambda$ of shape and type $\lambda$, its refinement fibre consists just of $t^\lambda$, so $m_{T^\lambda T^\lambda}=m_\lambda$. Accordingly $\varphi_{T^\lambda T^\lambda}$ is the identity on $M^\lambda$ and zero on other summands; it is the genuine projection $1_\lambda$. Squaring it gives $1_\lambda^2=1_\lambda$. In the free shape-$\lambda$ cell quotient, the cell product is $1_\lambda^2\equiv B_\lambda(\varphi_{T^\lambda},\varphi_{T^\lambda})1_\lambda$, and the coefficient of this basis vector is therefore $1$. Over a field this form is not identically zero. Step 4.1 and [F4] consequently show that every $W^\lambda$ has the nonzero absolutely simple head $L^\lambda$, that these heads give all simple modules exactly once, and that the stated diagonal and dominance decomposition conditions hold. [step 2.1, step 4.1, F4, algebra]

6.1 Weight ranks and edge cases. Direct summand projections $1_
u$ satisfy the displayed orthogonality and sum-to-one relations. The source support of $\varphi_{ST}$ implies $\varphi_{ST}1_
u=\delta_{\operatorname{type}(T),
u}\varphi_{ST}$, so the same formula holds on the right Weyl cell basis, proving its weight rank $K_{\lambda
u}$. It asserts no idempotence for other cellular diagonal elements. Deleting empty rows leaves the Young subgroup unchanged and identifies the row-type fibres after the order-preserving relabelling of the remaining row labels; hence all constructions allow zero parts. At $n=0$ the unique empty tableau and empty partition give $H=R$, $S=R$ and cell form $1$. If $d=0<n$, the indexing set of weak compositions and the direct sum are empty, $S=0$, and every basis and simple-label assertion is empty. No division except by powers of the unit $q$, generic semisimplicity or choice principle enters any step. [given, step 2.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

In the generic type-A Hecke algebra $H_v(n)$ over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ with
generators $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$, the quadratic relations
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, the braid relations and the distant commutations, and with
$T_w$ the product of the $T_i$ along a reduced word for $w\in S_n$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]):

1. $\{T_w:w\in S_n\}$ is an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$; in particular $H_v(n)$ is
free of rank $n!$ over $A$;
2. for every $w\in S_n$ and every $1\le i\le n-1$,
$$T_wT_i=T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1,\qquad T_wT_i=(v-1)T_w+v\,T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)-1,$$
where $\ell$ is the inversion length of $S_n$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]); consequently the rule rewrites
every monomial in the generators as an $A$-linear combination of the $T_w$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, and $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ with
standard basis $\{T_w\}$ and star anti-automorphism $*$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]],
[[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]],
[[lem-the-star-antiautomorphism-of-the-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). For a
composition (in particular a partition) $\mu$ of $n$ put
$m_\mu:=\sum_{w\in S_\mu}T_w\in H$, the **row symmetrizer** of the standard
Young subgroup $S_\mu$
([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]]); the sum has
$|S_\mu|=\prod_i\mu_i!$ terms.

A tableau is **row standard** when its entries increase along each row. Use the right tableau action $t\cdot w:=w^{-1}\cdot t$, where the left action applies $w$ to the entries. For a row-standard $\mu$-tableau $s$, let $d(s)$ be the unique permutation with $s=t^\mu\cdot d(s)$, where $t^\mu$ is filled by $1,2,\dots,n$ in row-major order. Explicitly, if $s$ carries entry $a$ in the $p$-th node in that order, then $d(s)(a)=p$: $d(s)$ is the **inverse** of the row-reading permutation. The action on tableaux is free; the stabilizer of the row tabloid of $t^\mu$ is $S_\mu$ ([[def-row-and-column-stabilizers-of-a-tableau]]).

Write $D_\mu$ for these distinguished permutations. Row-standardness says that $d^{-1}$ is increasing on each canonical row block. The coset $S_\mu d$ consists exactly of the tableaux with the same row sets, so sorting each row produces its unique representative in $D_\mu$. Moreover,
$$\ell(wd)=\ell(w)+\ell(d)\qquad(w\in S_\mu,\ d\in D_\mu).$$
To verify this, count inversions of $(wd)^{-1}=d^{-1}w^{-1}$. Pairs of labels within one canonical block contribute exactly the inversions of $w^{-1}$, since $d^{-1}$ is increasing there. For labels in different blocks, $w^{-1}$ permutes the labels within their respective blocks, so the total number of cross-block inversions equals that of $d^{-1}$. The two contributions give the displayed equality, using inversion invariance of length. It also proves minimality and uniqueness in $S_\mu d$. These conventions extend to compositions by using their consecutive row blocks.
For row-standard $\mu$-tableaux $s,t$ define the **Murphy element**
$$m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^{*}\,m_{\mu}\,T_{d(t)}\in H,$$
and for a standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$ shorten
$m_t:=m_{tt}=T_{d(t)}^{*}m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$. Then $m_{st}^{*}=m_{ts}$ for all
row-standard $s,t$ of the same shape: applying the anti-automorphism, which
fixes $m_\mu$ because $m_\mu^*=\sum_{w\in S_\mu}T_{w^{-1}}=m_\mu$, gives
$$m_{st}^{*}=(T_{d(s)}^{*}m_\mu T_{d(t)})^{*}=T_{d(t)}^{*}m_\mu^{*}T_{d(s)}^{**}=T_{d(t)}^{*}m_\mu T_{d(s)}=m_{ts}.$$
Finally, $m_\mu T_w=q^{\ell(w)}m_\mu$ for every $w\in S_\mu$: it suffices to
prove this for $w=s_i$ a simple transposition with $i,i+1$ in the same block of
$\mu$, since any $w\in S_\mu\setminus\{1\}$ has a reduced expression
$w=w's_i$ with $\ell(w)=\ell(w')+1$ and the claim follows by induction,
$m_\mu T_w=m_\mu T_{w'}T_i=q^{\ell(w')}m_\mu T_i=q^{\ell(w)}m_\mu$. For such
$i$ the right multiplication $v\mapsto vs_i$ is an involution of the finite
group $S_\mu$, and pairing the summands of $m_\mu T_i=\sum_{v\in S_\mu}T_vT_i$
in twos gives, in the two cases of the standard-basis multiplication rule
$T_vT_i=T_{vs_i}$ if $\ell(vs_i)=\ell(v)+1$ and
$T_vT_i=(q-1)T_v+qT_{vs_i}$ if $\ell(vs_i)=\ell(v)-1$,
$$T_vT_i+T_{vs_i}T_i=q\,(T_v+T_{vs_i}),$$
so summing over the $\tfrac12|S_\mu|$ pairs yields $m_\mu T_i=qm_\mu$.

For every commutative ring $R$ with invertible parameter $z$, the ordinary
finite type-A Hecke algebra $H_n$ and a composition $\rho$ of $n$, the
permutation module $x_\rho H_n$ has $R$-basis
$$m_{(S,t)}=\sum_{s:\,\rho(s)=S}m_{st},$$
where $S$ ranges over the semistandard tableaux of partition shape and type
$\rho$ and $t$ over the standard tableaux of the same shape. It has a Specht
filtration with multiplicity $\#\operatorname{SStd}_\rho(\lambda)$ of the
ordinary Specht module $S^\lambda$
([[def-semistandard-tableau-and-kostka-number]],
[[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]). The row-double-coset
membership uses each coset word once and no quantum-factorial division. Over
the generic field this number equals the trivial-character multiplicity of the
$\rho$-row parabolic in $S^\lambda$. Moreover the explicit ordinary Garnir
row-coset identity, the additive nonstandard-tableau factorization and the
same-column generator refinement
$$T_am_{st}\equiv-m_{st}+\sum_{u\lhd s}c_um_{ut}\pmod{\text{higher shapes}}$$
hold; row-standard straightening has no smaller-shape terms and its same-shape
terms increase tableau-prefix dominance. Shape support uses the already proved
ordinary Murphy dominance ideals
([[thm-murphy-tableau-elements-form-a-cellular-basis]],
[[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]); the finite Garnir
algorithm terminates in lexicographic shape/tableau order before that
dominance refinement.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, and $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Let $\Lambda$ be the set of partitions
of $n$ ordered by dominance $\unrhd$
([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]), and for $\lambda\in\Lambda$ let
$T(\lambda)=\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)$ be the set of standard $\lambda$-tableaux
([[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]). Then the **Murphy basis
theorem** holds: the family
$$\mathcal M=\{m_{st}:\lambda\vdash n,\ s,t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)\}$$
is an $R$-basis of $H$, and $(\mathcal M,\Lambda)$ is a cellular basis of $H$ in
the sense of [[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]. Explicitly:
(i) $m_{st}^{*}=m_{ts}$ for all $\lambda$ and $s,t$; and (ii) for every
$\lambda$, every $t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)$ and every $h\in H$ there exist
$r_v\in R$ with
$$m_{st}h\equiv\sum_{v\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)}r_v\,m_{sv}\pmod{H^{\rhd\lambda}},$$
where $H^{\rhd\lambda}$ is spanned by the $m_{uv}$ with $\mu\rhd\lambda$. The
theorem holds over every commutative coefficient ring with $q\in R^{\times}$
and assumes no semisimplicity; the total number of Murphy elements is
$\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}|\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)|^2=n!$
([[cor-sum-of-squares-of-standard-tableau-numbers]]), matching the rank of $H$.

Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital cellular $F$-algebra with
cellular basis $(C,\Lambda)$ over the finite poset $\Lambda$
([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]). For $\lambda\in\Lambda$
put $D^{\lambda}:=C^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$, where
$\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the radical of the cell form
([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]). Then:

1. if $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ then $D^{\lambda}$ is an absolutely irreducible
   (absolutely simple) $A$-module: it is simple over $F$ and remains simple
   after every extension of scalars to a larger field;
2. $\{D^{\lambda}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ D^{\lambda}\ne0\}$ is a complete set of
   pairwise non-isomorphic simple $A$-modules ([[def-simple-module]],
   [[thm-jordan-holder-theorem-for-modules]]);
3. $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ if and only if the cell form
   $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda$ is not identically zero, if and only if
   $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}\ne C^{\lambda}$; and, when these equivalent
   conditions hold, $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the unique maximal proper
   submodule and the Jacobson radical of $C^{\lambda}$, so $D^{\lambda}$ is its
   simple head. If the form is identically zero, the cell-form quotient
   $D^{\lambda}$ is zero; no assertion about the Jacobson radical or the actual
   head of $C^{\lambda}$ is made.

No semisimplicity of $A$ is assumed; the theorem is the Graham-Lehrer
classification and applies in particular to $A=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ for every field
$F$ and every $q\in F^{\times}$.

Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional cellular algebra over a field $F$
([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]) with cell modules
$C_\lambda$ and cell-form quotients $D_\lambda=C_\lambda/R_\lambda$. Then:

1. every nonzero $D_\lambda$ is an absolutely simple head, all simple
   $A$-modules occur exactly once this way, and $[C_\lambda:D_\mu]\ne0$ implies
   $\lambda\ge\mu$, with $[C_\mu:D_\mu]=1$ whenever $D_\mu\ne0$; here
   "nonzero quotient" means nonzero form, not necessarily a nondegenerate form
   on $C_\lambda$;
2. every nonzero cell module, including labels with zero-form quotient, has
   all its composition factors in a single block
   ([[def-blocks-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]);
3. two nonzero cell modules share a block exactly when they are linked by a
   finite chain of nonzero cell modules whose neighbouring terms share a
   simple composition factor;
4. for one primitive idempotent $e_\mu$ per simple,
   $$\dim_Fe_\mu Ae_\nu=\sum_\lambda[C_\lambda:D_\mu]\,[C_\lambda:D_\nu].$$

If the cellular index set $T(\lambda)$ is empty, then $C_\lambda=D_\lambda=0$.
Its block support, the set of primitive central idempotents $b$ with
$C_\lambda b\ne0$, is empty, and it has no simple composition factors.
It does not participate in the nonzero-cell linkage criterion of (3), and
its term in the corner sum of (4) is zero.

def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-f.body:
## Definition

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$, let $q\in R^{\times}$, let $d,n\ge0$ with $d\ge n$, and let $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Write $S:=S(d,n)=\mathrm{End}_H(M)$ for the type-A q-Schur algebra with $M=\bigoplus_{\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)}M^{\mu}$ the direct sum of the permutation modules ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]], [[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]]) and let $\{\varphi_{ST}:\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n),\ S,T\in T_0(\lambda)\}$ be its cellular semistandard basis ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]] for the underlying Murphy elements and [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] for the standard basis along which this basis is defined). Put $\omega:=(1^n,0^{d-n})\in\Lambda(d,n)$, the length-$d$ composition with $n$ entries equal to $1$ (legitimate because $d\ge n$), so that the Young subgroup $S_\omega$ is trivial and $m_\omega=1$; hence $$M^{\omega}=m_\omega H=H$$ is the regular right $H$-module. Let $t^{\omega}$ be the unique standard $\omega$-tableau, with entries $1,2,\dots,n$ down its single column; it is in particular the unique row-standard $\omega$-tableau whose entries increase down the column. Set $$e:=\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}\in S.$$

Then:

1. $e$ is the projection of $M$ onto the direct summand $M^{\omega}=H$ along the other summands $M^{\mu}$, $\mu\ne\omega$; in particular $e^2=e$ and $$eSe\cong\mathrm{End}_H(M^{\omega})=\mathrm{End}_H(H),$$ via the algebra isomorphism $$\rho:H\longrightarrow eSe,\qquad h\longmapsto\rho_h,\qquad \rho_h(x):=hx,$$ left multiplication by $h$ on $M^{\omega}=H$ being a right $H$-module endomorphism. Here the isomorphism $eSe\cong\mathrm{End}_H(M^{\omega})$ sends $efe$ to $f|_{M^{\omega}}$ and is inverted by extending an endomorphism of $M^{\omega}$ by zero on the other summands, and the identification $\mathrm{End}_H(H)\cong H$ sends an endomorphism to its value at $1$. By the construction of the semistandard basis elements $\varphi_{ST}$ (Mathas (4.13) with Corollaries 4.9 and 4.12; see the locator above), the diagonal element $\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}$ is exactly the endomorphism of $M$ that is the identity on $M^{\omega}$ and zero on all $M^{\mu}$ with $\mu\ne\omega$, which is the projection asserted above.

2. The **Schur functor** is $$F:\mathrm{mod}\text{-}S\longrightarrow\mathrm{mod}\text{-}H,\qquad F(X):=Xe=X\otimes_SSe,$$ with the right $H$-action transported along $\rho$, so that $(xe)\cdot h:=x\,\rho_h$ for $x\in X$, $h\in H$ ([[def-left-and-right-modules]]). It is exact and $R$-linear on morphisms: as a **left** $S$-module, $Se$ is the image of the left-$S$-linear projection $s\mapsto se$ on $S$, hence is a direct summand of the regular left module and is projective. Tensoring right $S$-modules with this left module is therefore exact. Equivalently, for a short exact sequence of right modules, an element $ye$ in the target lifts to $xe$ from any lift $x$ of $y$; kernels and injections are likewise preserved by the same idempotent projection. The bimodule corner action makes these maps right $H$-linear. The convention is fixed: the functor is $X\mapsto Xe$ on the right, and the left-module formula $X\mapsto eX$ is not used on this page.

thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-.body:
## Statement

Let $k$ be a field, $q\in k^\times$, $d\ge n$, and let $\mathcal F(X)=Xe$ be the right-module Schur functor of [[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]]. Set $e_q=e(k,q)$ ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]). For each $\lambda\in\Lambda^+(d,n)$ let $W^\lambda$ be the Weyl module with Schur cell form $B_\lambda$ and nonzero simple head $L^\lambda$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). Write $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ and $D_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ for the independent Murphy cell module and its cell-form quotient ([[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal F(W^\lambda)\cong C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ as right $H$-modules, and this isomorphism identifies $B_\lambda|_{W^\lambda e}$ exactly with the Murphy cell form. 2. $\mathcal F(L^\lambda)\cong D_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$, including the zero quotient; it is nonzero exactly when $\lambda$ is $e_q$-restricted. 3. For every $e_q$-restricted $\nu\vdash n$, $$[W^\lambda:L^\nu]=[C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda):D_{\mathrm M}(\nu)].$$

In the page's ordinary Dipper–James normalization ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]], [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]), these identities become $$\mathcal F(W^{\lambda'})\cong(S^\lambda)^\theta,\qquad \mathcal F(L^{\lambda'})\cong(D^\lambda)^\theta.$$ The latter module is nonzero exactly for $e_q$-regular $\lambda$ and is zero otherwise. For $e_q$-regular $\nu$, $$[W^{\lambda'}:L^{\nu'}]=[S^\lambda:D^\nu].$$ The accepted ordinary polytabloid comparison identifies $S^\lambda$ with the historical DJ module $P(\lambda)$ and identifies their form radicals through an explicit unit factor. Thus the dictionary concerns the actual ordinary modules, not merely a renamed cell module. A zero Hecke cell-form quotient is not asserted to be its actual module head. No semisimplicity or choice principle is assumed, and $n=0$ is included.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The field, parameter, stable range and modules in the Statement; all modules are right modules and multiplication in $S=\operatorname{End}_H(M)$ is ordinary composition $(fg)(x)=f(g(x))$.

[F1] The actual projection $e$ onto $M^\omega=H$, for $\omega=(1^n,0^{d-n})$, satisfies $e^2=e$ and $eSe\cong H$ by left multiplication $\rho(h)(a)=ha$. The functor is $X\mapsto Xe$ ([[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]]).

[F2] The legitimate semistandard cellular construction is supported from $M^{\operatorname{type}(T)}$ to $M^{\operatorname{type}(S)}$ and sends its generating $m_{\operatorname{type}(T)}h$ to $m_{ST}h$; its star swaps $S,T$ and its right-cell coefficients fix the first index modulo higher shapes. The Weyl cell basis is $(w_T)_T$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). Only the actual summand projections are weight idempotents; no assertion that all diagonal cellular elements are idempotent is used.

[F3] The independent Murphy cellular datum uses $m_{st}=T_{d(s)}^*x_\lambda T_{d(t)}$, with its higher ideal $I^{\rhd\lambda}$, right cell basis $(c_t)_t$ and form $G_\lambda$ characterized by $m_{as}m_{tb}\equiv G_\lambda(c_s,c_t)m_{ab}$ modulo that ideal ([[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]]).

[F4] The nonzero cell-form quotients are pairwise distinct absolutely irreducible modules; when the form is not identically zero its radical is the unique maximal submodule. These are the general cellular conclusions of [[thm-nonzero-cell-heads-classify-the-simple-modules-of-a-cellular-algebra]].

[F5] The genuine ordinary bridge gives $P(\alpha)\cong C_{\mathrm M}(\alpha')^\theta$ and an explicit unit-scaled form identity, hence $D_{\mathrm{DJ}}(\alpha)\cong D_{\mathrm M}(\alpha')^\theta$ including zero quotients. This is the page's signed Specht normalization, and $\theta$ is an involutive algebra automorphism whose pullback is exact ([[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]], [[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]).

[F6] The full type-A classifier proves that $D_{\mathrm M}(\nu)$ is nonzero precisely for $e_q$-restricted $\nu$ over the original field, including the finite-$e_q$ range and the empty partition; its ordinary-label statement is transported through the signed-conjugate form bridge, not inferred from a group-only specialization ([[thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]], [[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Under [F1], $\rho(h)\rho(k)=\rho(hk)$ because both act on $H$ by left multiplication, so the identification uses $H$, without an opposite algebra. The functor $X\mapsto Xe$ is exact: for a short exact sequence, a lift $x$ of an element $y\in X''e$ yields the lift $xe$, and an element in the kernel lies in $X'$ and is fixed by $e$, hence lies in $X'e$. The tensor description uses the $(S,eSe)$-bimodule $Se$, which is a direct summand as a left $S$-module. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 The support in [F2] gives $e\varphi_{ST}e=\delta_{\operatorname{type}(S),\omega}\delta_{\operatorname{type}(T),\omega}\varphi_{ST}$ and $w_Te=\delta_{\operatorname{type}(T),\omega}w_T$. Semistandard tableaux of type $\omega$ have each label once and are exactly standard tableaux. For standard $s,t$, their defining sum $m_{st}$ has one term, so $\varphi_{st}|_H(a)=m_{st}a$ and $\rho^{-1}(\varphi_{st})=m_{st}$. Thus the higher Schur ideal cuts out exactly $I^{\rhd\lambda}$ in the corner. Read the Schur right-cell law with first index any standard tableau of type $\omega$; coefficient independence permits this choice. Restricting the multiplication by $\rho(h)$ to $H$ gives $m_{st}h$, so its coefficients are the Murphy right-cell coefficients. Consequently $\Psi_\lambda:W^\lambda e\to C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$, $w_t\mapsto c_t$, is an $H$-isomorphism. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 By the Schur cell product, $\varphi_{as}\varphi_{tb}\equiv B_\lambda(w_s,w_t)\varphi_{ab}$ modulo higher Schur shapes, with coefficient independent of the outer indices. Choose all four indices standard of shape $\lambda$ and type $\omega$. They lie in $eSe$; applying $\rho^{-1}$, or evaluating their endomorphisms at $1\in H$, gives $m_{as}m_{tb}\equiv B_\lambda(w_s,w_t)m_{ab}$ modulo $I^{\rhd\lambda}$. The unique coefficient in [F3] is $G_\lambda(c_s,c_t)$, proving $B_\lambda|_{W^\lambda e}=\Psi_\lambda^*G_\lambda$ exactly, with factor $1$. [F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Since $e^*=e$, contravariance gives $B_\lambda(xe,y(1-e))=B_\lambda(x,y(1-e)e)=0$. The decomposition $W^\lambda=W^\lambda e\oplus W^\lambda(1-e)$ is therefore orthogonal. A vector in $W^\lambda e$ pairs trivially with its complement, so it is in the restricted form radical exactly when it lies in $\operatorname{rad}_{\mathrm{form}}W^\lambda$. Since the latter is an $S$-submodule, $\operatorname{rad}_{\mathrm{form}}(W^\lambda e)=(\operatorname{rad}_{\mathrm{form}}W^\lambda)e$. This holds even if the corner form is identically zero. [F2, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 For the canonical semistandard tableau $T^\lambda$ of shape and type $\lambda$, the map $\varphi_{T^\lambda,T^\lambda}$ is the actual projection onto $M^\lambda$: it sends $m_\lambda h$ to itself and is zero on every other summand. Its square equals itself, so the Schur cell product gives $B_\lambda(w_{T^\lambda},w_{T^\lambda})=1$. Hence the Weyl form quotient is nonzero and is its simple head $L^\lambda$ by [F4]. Exactness, step 4.1 and step 3.1 give $L^\lambda e\cong W^\lambda e/(\operatorname{rad}_{\mathrm{form}}W^\lambda)e\cong C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)/\operatorname{rad}_{\mathrm{form}}C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)=D_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$, including when this corner quotient is zero. [F2, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 By [F6] and step 5.1, $L^\lambda e\ne0$ precisely for $e_q$-restricted $\lambda$. Apply the exact functor to a finite composition series of $W^\lambda$: every factor $L^\nu$ gives $D_{\mathrm M}(\nu)$ or zero. Delete repeated terms. The remaining factors are the distinct nonzero Murphy simples in [F4], giving $[W^\lambda:L^\nu]=[C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda):D_{\mathrm M}(\nu)]$ for each $e_q$-restricted $\nu$. No multiplicity preservation is asserted for a killed simple label. [F4, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 Apply [F5] and the involution $\theta$ to obtain $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')\cong(S^\lambda)^\theta$ and $D_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')\cong(D^\lambda)^\theta$. Replacing the Weyl label by $\lambda'$ in steps 2.1 and 5.1 gives the ordinary dictionary, including zero quotients. Conjugation makes $\lambda'$ restricted precisely when $\lambda$ is regular. Twisting both modules by the same exact equivalence preserves composition multiplicities, so step 6.1 gives $[W^{\lambda'}:L^{\nu'}]=[S^\lambda:D^\nu]$ for regular $\nu$. The genuine unit-scaled ordinary form bridge in [F5] also identifies these with the historical DJ polytabloid modules and quotients. At $n=0$, $e=1$ and each form has value $1$, so the same proof includes the empty partition. [F4, F5, F6, step 2.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, algebra] ∎

cex-cellularity-does-not-make-every-cell.body:
## Statement refuted

A cellular algebra need not be semisimple, its cell modules need not be simple, and a labelled cell-form quotient $D^{\lambda}$ may vanish although the cell module $C^{\lambda}$ is nonzero.

(a) Abstract degenerate instance: let $F$ be a field and $A=F[x]/(x^2)$, with $\Lambda=\{2\rhd1\}$ ordered so that $2\rhd1$, cellular basis $c_{11}:=1$ in cell $1$ and $c_{22}:=x$ in cell $2$ and $i=\mathrm{id}$ ([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]). For $a+bx\in A$ one has $1(a+bx)\equiv a\cdot1\pmod{(x)}$ and $x(a+bx)=ax$, so the triangular axiom holds, and $A^{\rhd1}=(x)$, $A^{\rhd2}=0$. The cell form on $C^{2}$ has $c_{22}c_{22}=x^2=0$, so it is identically zero, $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{2}=C^{2}$ and $D^{2}=0$, while both $C^{1}$ and $C^{2}$ are one-dimensional simple modules: on either, $a+bx$ acts as the scalar $a$. In particular the Jacobson radical of $C^{2}$ is zero and its actual head is $C^{2}$, even though its cell-form radical is all of $C^{2}$ and its cell-form quotient is zero: cellularity does not force $D^{\lambda}\ne0$, and the algebra is not semisimple since $\mathrm{rad}\,A=(x)$.

(b) Hecke instance: let $F$ be a field of characteristic $2$ and $q=1$, so $e=\operatorname{char}(F)=2$ ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]); for $n=3$ and $\lambda=(1,1,1)$ the partition $(1,1,1)$ is not $2$-regular ([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]), so $D^{(1,1,1)}=0$ while the page's Specht module $S^{(1,1,1)}\cong D^{(3)}$ is the nonzero trivial module (in characteristic $2$ the sign module is trivial) ([[thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]], [[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]).

(c) Reducible cell module: in the $F=\mathbb C$, $q=-1$, $e=2$ specialization of the example the q-Schur cell module $W^{(3,2)}_F$ satisfies $\sum_{i>0}[W^{(3,2)}_F(i)]=[L^{(3,1^2)}_F]+2[L^{(2^2,1)}_F]\ne0$ ([[thm-q-schaper-virtual-radical-layer-formula]], the calculation of [[ex-q-schaper-for-shape-three-two-at-e-two]]), so its radical is nonzero and $W^{(3,2)}_F$ is reducible even though it has a simple head.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The three settings above: the algebra $A=F[x]/(x^2)$, the Hecke algebra $H_{F,q}(S_3)$ in characteristic $2$ at $q=1$, and the q-Schur Weyl module $W^{(3,2)}_F$ over $F=\mathbb C$, $q=-1$, at $e=2$.

[F1] ([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]], [[thm-nonzero-cell-heads-classify-the-simple-modules-of-a-cellular-algebra]]) For a cellular basis, products of two elements of the smaller cell vanish modulo the larger cell exactly when the corresponding form entry vanishes; $D^{\lambda}=C^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is zero if and only if the cell form is identically zero, and only in the nonzero case is $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ the module-theoretic Jacobson radical and the head quotient.

[F2] The actual Murphy cell form is defined by the coefficient in $m_{as}m_{tb}$, and the signed-conjugate ordinary bridge transports its radical through a unit-scaled form identity ([[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]], [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]). At $q=1$ in characteristic $2$, the sign twist acts trivially and the quantum characteristic is $2$.

[F3] ([[thm-q-schaper-virtual-radical-layer-formula]], [[ex-q-schaper-for-shape-three-two-at-e-two]]) For the specified $F=\mathbb C$, $q=-1$ lift with $e=2$, the positive Jantzen submodule sum for $W^{(3,2)}_F$ is $[L^{(3,1^2)}_F]+2[L^{(2^2,1)}_F]\ne0$.




## Counterexample

1.1 The abstract instance: in $A=F[x]/(x^2)$ with $c_{11}=1$, $c_{22}=x$ and $2\rhd1$, the product $c_{22}c_{22}=x^2=0$ is congruent to $0\cdot c_{22}$ modulo $A^{\rhd2}=0$, so the axiom holds with zero form value; the products $c_{11}(a+bx)=a+bx\equiv a\,c_{11}\pmod{(x)}$ and $c_{22}(a+bx)=ax=a\,c_{22}$ confirm the triangularity. Hence $C^{2}$ has identically zero form, $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{2}=C^{2}$ and $D^{2}=0$; the module $C^{2}$ itself is one-dimensional with $a+bx$ acting as $a$, hence simple with zero Jacobson radical and head $C^{2}\ne0$. Moreover $a+bx$ is a unit exactly when $a\ne0$: in that case its inverse is $a^{-1}-ba^{-2}x$, while every element of $(x)$ squares to zero. Thus $(x)$ is the unique maximal ideal, so $\operatorname{rad}A=(x)\ne0$. The regular module is not semisimple: its submodule $(x)$ has no complementary ideal, since any nonzero ideal meeting $A\setminus(x)$ contains a unit and equals $A$. [given, F1]

1.2 The Hecke instance directly. At $q=1$, put $x=\sum_{w\in S_3}T_w$. Pairing terms gives $xT_i=x$, and multiplication gives $x^2=6x=0$ in characteristic $2$. The top Murphy cell is the free rank-one row-character module generated by $x$, and there is no higher shape than $(3)$; hence its cell form has value $6=0$ and its labelled quotient is zero. The signed-conjugate bridge in [F2] identifies the ordinary module $S^{(1,1,1)}$ and its form radical with this Murphy cell and its radical, through a unit factor. Since the sign twist is trivial in characteristic $2$, this is the nonzero trivial module, while $D^{(1,1,1)}=0$. Thus this witness does not require the general finite-quantum-characteristic classifier. [given, F2, algebra]

1.3 The reducible Weyl module. In the precise lift of [F3], the sum of the positive filtration-submodule classes is $[L^{(3,1^2)}]+2[L^{(2,2,1)}]\ne0$. At least one of these submodules is nonzero. Since all are contained in the first reduced submodule $W_F(1)=\operatorname{rad}_{\rm form}W_F$, that radical is nonzero. The Schur cell form has nonzero simple head, so its form radical is its unique maximal proper submodule. Consequently $W_F^{(3,2)}$ is reducible, despite having simple head $L^{(3,2)}$. Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$ and $A$ a unital $R$-algebra
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) that is free as an $R$-module on a
finite set $C=\{c^{\lambda}_{st}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ s,t\in T(\lambda)\}$,
where $(\Lambda,\unrhd)$ is a finite poset ([[def-partial-order]]; its strict
order is written $\rhd$) and each $T(\lambda)$ is a finite set. For
$\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ be the $R$-submodule of $A$ spanned
by all $c^{\mu}_{uv}$ with $\mu\rhd\lambda$.

Then $(C,\Lambda)$ is a **cellular basis** of $A$, and $A$ is a **cellular
algebra**, if:

(i) the $R$-linear map $i:A\to A$ with $i(c^{\lambda}_{st})=c^{\lambda}_{ts}$
for all $\lambda,s,t$ is an algebra anti-automorphism of $A$, i.e. $i(ab)=i(b)i(a)$
and $i(1)=1$ (equivalently $i$ is an isomorphism of $A$ with the opposite
algebra; the displayed formula forces $i^2=\mathrm{id}$); and

(ii) for every $\lambda\in\Lambda$, every $t\in T(\lambda)$ and every $a\in A$
there exist coefficients $r_v\in R$ ($v\in T(\lambda)$), independent of $s$, such that for every $s\in T(\lambda)$
$$c^{\lambda}_{st}\,a\equiv\sum_{v\in T(\lambda)}r_v\,c^{\lambda}_{sv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}.$$

**Cell modules.** For $\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $C^{\lambda}$ be the free
$R$-module with basis $\{c^{\lambda}_t:=c^{\lambda}_{tt}:t\in T(\lambda)\}$;
condition (ii) makes $C^{\lambda}$ a right $A$-module by
$c^{\lambda}_t a:=\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_v$ when
$c^{\lambda}_{tt}a\equiv\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_{tv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$, and
it makes $C^{\lambda}$ a left $A$-module via $i$, the left action being
$a\cdot c^{\lambda}_t:=c^{\lambda}_t\,i(a)$. Both actions are well defined on
the freely spanning basis elements by (ii): the coefficients $r_v$ are unique
because $C$ is an $R$-basis of $A$ and the quotient by $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ kills
exactly the basis elements indexed by strictly larger labels, while applying
the anti-automorphism (i) to (ii) gives the same triangularity for left
multiplication. The module $C^{\lambda}$ is the **(right) cell module** of
$\lambda$, and
$$A^{\unrhd\lambda}/A^{\rhd\lambda}\cong C^{\lambda}\otimes_R C^{\lambda}$$
via $c^{\lambda}_{st}+A^{\rhd\lambda}\mapsto c^{\lambda}_s\otimes c^{\lambda}_t$,
where $A^{\unrhd\lambda}$ is spanned by all $c^{\mu}_{uv}$ with
$\mu\unrhd\lambda$. A cellular algebra may have several cellular bases.

Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital cellular $F$-algebra with
cellular basis $(C,\Lambda)$ over the finite poset $\Lambda$
([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]). For $\lambda\in\Lambda$
put $D^{\lambda}:=C^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$, where
$\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the radical of the cell form
([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]). Then:

1. if $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ then $D^{\lambda}$ is an absolutely irreducible
   (absolutely simple) $A$-module: it is simple over $F$ and remains simple
   after every extension of scalars to a larger field;
2. $\{D^{\lambda}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ D^{\lambda}\ne0\}$ is a complete set of
   pairwise non-isomorphic simple $A$-modules ([[def-simple-module]],
   [[thm-jordan-holder-theorem-for-modules]]);
3. $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ if and only if the cell form
   $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda$ is not identically zero, if and only if
   $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}\ne C^{\lambda}$; and, when these equivalent
   conditions hold, $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the unique maximal proper
   submodule and the Jacobson radical of $C^{\lambda}$, so $D^{\lambda}$ is its
   simple head. If the form is identically zero, the cell-form quotient
   $D^{\lambda}$ is zero; no assertion about the Jacobson radical or the actual
   head of $C^{\lambda}$ is made.

No semisimplicity of $A$ is assumed; the theorem is the Graham-Lehrer
classification and applies in particular to $A=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ for every field
$F$ and every $q\in F^{\times}$.

For every commutative ring $R$, every $q\in R^\times$, and every partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ with row symmetrizer $m_\lambda=x_\lambda$, put
$m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^*m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$ for standard $\lambda$-tableaux $s,t$,
where $d(t)\in D_\lambda$ is the element with $t^\lambda\cdot d(t)=t$. Then:

1. $\{m_{st}:\lambda\vdash n,\ s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$ is an
$R$-basis of $H$ (the **Murphy basis**), and $m_{st}^*=m_{ts}$.

2. The $R$-spans $I^{\unrhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\unrhd\lambda\}$ and
$I^{\rhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\rhd\lambda\}$ are two-sided ideals of $H$
(dominance order), and $I^{\unrhd\lambda}/I^{\rhd\lambda}$ is free with basis

with basis $\{m_t:=x_\lambda T_{d(t)}+I^{\rhd\lambda}:t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$

$G_\lambda(m_sh,m_t)=G_\lambda(m_s,m_th^*)$, and its radical is a submodule of
